## Design

### 2026-10-21 – I have spent the last half hour planning out what the keyboard whould look like and what basic functionality it should have.

**0.5h**

I have spent the last half hour planning out what the keyboard whould look like and what basic functionality it should have.

This is the plan so far.

![1000102602](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/c95a8288adb5c3206074f1b1005af853437dde317b87c051b6c6612cb0620c05.jpg)

![1000102601](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/aba2df2ab32f7d9db3e3cc789c1d4060d583e4170126faea8009ac8387df4fc1.jpg)

Originally my plan was to add more fun effects such as eq. However as this is a MIDI device and the sound comes from a different device, wave forms cannot be altered. Therefore I would not be able to implement eq.

The two octaves allows me freely move through the entire range of a piano with an octave jump which assures that I will be able to move through ranges effectively.

The instrument change button will allow me to cycle through instruments that are available through midi which can be set beforehand, so that I can loop through them.

Volume (written as gain) will not actually be able to used as gain because there is no voltage gain in the signal all it will be able to do is tell the controller that the volume should be higher which will signal to a secondary device that the volume should be higher.

### 2026-10-21 – Starting to put this keyboard together, I started by dowloading all the libraries and adding their configuration for schematics, footprints and 3D models.

**1h**

Starting to put this keyboard together, I started by dowloading all the libraries and adding their configuration for schematics, footprints and 3D models.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/9deb952baf560a9f71a5b45ca37f8371276a73018fe990db0fb794ab66fa9397.png)

However even at the very start I realised a big issue witht the way I had designed my keyboard:
 - There were 2 octaves of 12 keys and an extra c (for musical standard)
 - And there were 3 buttons, for octave change up and down as well as instrument change
 - There was also a volume encoder.

This means that I would need 29 GPIOs which was obviously not available in the seeduino or the Waveshare.

I could... buy a bigger device with more inputs (likely 30) however I asked AI to see what other methods could be used.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/a799690a9a343bca0957767b230f8a50cd0b943ccbdfc79b1e7967659422eac4.png)

One method that I was shown was using matrices which I was more familiar with as well as adding a component labelled the MCP23017 which would add on an extra 16 inputs.

Using matrices would already allow me to design the keys as a 5 * 5 thus 25 keys and a 10 inputs and thus much less.

The total amount of inputs that I would have needed would therefore be:
 - 10 + 3 + 1 = 14

Though this would wtill be too many for the original seeduino, I could use the MCP23017 to add more inputs and have a max amount of:
 - 11 (for seeduino inputs) + 16 (for additional MCP) - 2 (scl and scd) which would give me 30 inputs.

Though I could easily just attach all inputs just by adding the extension. For the purposes of fun I am going to continue using the matrices approach.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/2fa9cfc5c7d77f7570fcdd707a14fc502b9ba45f8258d88445ef467f5a98a708.png)

However I then realised that the rotary encoder would firstly need 2 inputs for the rotary encoder and therefore I would 30 inputs and AI had advised a better move.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/70fc464b0ec1709e9cddaa7c84c81f4807b92d5f0f4f95227c92e946f9e348a0.png)

This would be bad but then I could use a 5 by 6 matrix and only have to use 11 pins. This would just about fit into the xiao meaning I would not need to use any other chips such as the MCP23017 but I could do things just on the XIAO.

Knowing this, I knew what would be need on the schematic and that I would need to learn matrices soon. However that meant tha I could carry on setting up the microcontroller with its power buttons.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/d85a466a6efc8b9b144b3df19ab188ad6731f4dd89aefdae842ef3b22d5fb717.png)

Now that everything is planned out I can add all the sections I might want.

### 2026-10-22 – Here I learnt about how to apply matrices in electronics using the guide I found on the github repo so I could add all 30 of my switches without issue. However I then cam across this:

**0.5h**

Here I learnt about how to apply matrices in electronics using the guide I found on the github repo so I could add all 30 of my switches without issue. However I then cam across this:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/351dfeb85ce871761186a47aafcd7a40e16bfe9f2b517d91bb1ad18d347a1e98.png)

I had not realised while planning that not all GPIO pins would be able to support capacitative touch and therefore my use of matrices would not work. To figure this out I asked AI:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/41b558703cb9fce0dcea9ea0f01fcf0e42a833b1665f85ede2015c4838110103.png)

However by asking AI I realised that matrices would be an effective method of doing this if these were regular switches. The nature of the capactitative touch mechanism meant that I would need either another dedicated IC to be able to do this or I would need multiplexers.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/6d50be89bca192e229bd8e7f7dbc76d3b82eb684beccec7c59f5014a895027c8.png)

This would mean that I would need to be able to have 25 GPIOs just for keys, and I would not be able to utilise matrices for this unless I made them physical keys.

The cost for going through with this would come up to:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/7ddb423e0898e6d081d5b3ec0eeec76267ccb16a4b6dd8e1d3b6dcc5332e71f7.png)

roughly £13-22 which is very close to the edge of my limit considering I will need to pay for the cost of manufacture.

Realising that this idea of adding 2 octaves though much more realistic was not cost effective or within my skill level I knew I had to replan my idea.

The smallest reasonable size for an instrument would be diatonic 8 notes c-c with octave jump

This would mean I would have in total:
 - 8 capacitative keys
 - 1 rotary encoder (2 inputs)
 - 2 octave jump switches
 - 1 instument change button

8 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 13

This would be too many inputs for  an 11 pin microcontroller.

Realising this, I knew that the best method to develop this was to use the more expensive Waveshare ESP32-S3-Zero which would have 13 pins exactly the amount I would need.

Unfortunately this meant starting all my work from scratch again this time with a Waveshare ESP32-S3-Zero.

At this point I could just wire up the rest of the components linearly and I would have little to no issue but I wanted to see whether I could add any more functionality. I looked at having a ptch bend wheel online and realised the technical name is a "self centering potentiometer".

This mean that I would have no other useful functionality that I could add apart from a modulation key, However a one way modulation key would not prove very useful and I would either need to use a spring returning potentiometer to do this (and essentially use pitch bend) or use 2 buttons or other methods that would need 2 inputs. Considering my scarcity of GPIO inputs, I decided that this would not be a good idea to implement now but maybe afterwards.

Stage 6:
However as I was reading on:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/d699ecfaceedcd250b4386f2c5036c6536bb6948b1e0cb879f038c14fd69ec04.png)

This meant that I could also use another 2 inputs on my system which would mean I could have 15 inputs. I originally thought I might want to use this to make my system chromatic and have 12 keys at least. However with only 3 inputs left afterwards, this would not be able to store octave up down instrument change and volume knob. Therefore, I knew that I would not be able to use this system.

However this did mean that I could use a potentiometer with 2 inputs that would allow me to pitch bend. I first imagined using a rotary encoder for this function but it would have difficulty re-centering.

### 2026-10-22 – In this journal entry I developed my capacitative keys and further worked on the pcb.

**2h**

In this journal entry I developed my capacitative keys and further worked on the pcb.

Stage 1: (loading in pcb):

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/60c90f14fe114c8ed3c7fa48a6ef8a3a323d31a115276777fed9f0247219925a.png)

Stage2: (pads):
Since I am making this keyboard diatonic it would be silly for me to use the traditional keyboard layout with accidentals, instead I will replicate the layout with rectangular slabs.

As I am planning to be able to play this with my fingers (unless I have aluminium extensions) I wil need the slabs to be wide enough so that I can play these easily.

The contact area of my fingers specifically are 14mm wide therefore if I to add more leeway between keys 18mm will likely be enough for tolerances.

The average size of a piano key is 23.5mm so it is probably better to have wider piano keys in this instance.

For general use, I therefore think it would be better to use 22mm as I know that this is close to standard and will definitely be good enough for my fingers.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/ccc1e55270a789fb24d1ba0454b2357f3443d89d7a3059678c9565cf1e0dcf44.png)

Stage 3: (Saving to library and implementing with rest of board):

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/4c1abed17c01025eec127de83dcab4ae3b5d704c930f73b8bd9ac361932df533.png)

Stage 4:
I was asking a friend for help at this point and he pointed to me using lcsc and finding a plugin to be able to find footprints and convert lcsc into kicad.

After finding a method to be able to connect lcsc parts into kicad using python:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/93c0b8150444caa4915ae55e5255ab9977913275a8aa9b978e4e366063ecf7ce.png)

I went searching for a part that might fit the pitch bend component I so wanted.

AI had recommended I simply use a joystick and after a lot of searching for a suitable rotary encoder I couldn't find one.

After a long search on lcsc I found this which fit my requirements:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/86f3a8e5f62f3d1f793d417c8b3f58eb99f45997962808cd7e14e5c4d9bd43ce.png)

according to jlcpcb: https://jlcpcb.com/partdetail/YTL-YF16_ZL7_2_B5Kb_45_10_Y/C37323744 This would be self resetting (centering) and thus this would be perfect for me to use as a pitch bend

Now that I knew this I ran the software which allowed me to be able to extract these files and put them into my schematic.

Now the joystick was in the system:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/O3Acm6SNVObwxoygu6eLOTWIyDAUs5vl/a4e7a66b4492c8cd4e1d73e2a6bffd327dc527ecdb90b823593468e59d1997c2.png)
